Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) possess broad factual knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, but solving complex tasks also requires procedural knowledge about how to act. This paper introduces Procedural Atoms, fine-grained and independently applicable units that represent Intent, When, Do, and Avoid guidance. Building on this representation, we propose AtomSD, an Atom-guided Self-Distillation framework in which the learner continually extracts Procedural Atoms from its own successful trajectories and distills them into the evolving policy through Atom-conditioned supervision and task-reward optimization. Abstract: Large clinical language models often require multi-GPU infrastructure, limiting local deployment. Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks- MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K-1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

Abstract: Long-horizon language agents require compact memories that retain interaction evidence while preserving competing hypotheses about unobserved states. Although effective, many belief-state methods encode memory in discrete natural language, where repeated compression can omit evidence or prematurely discard plausible alternatives. We introduce LAMB, a recurrent framework for latent multi-hypothesis beliefs. A Common--Delta factorization combines a shared Common state for interaction evidence with weighted Delta components for competing hypotheses. Relative evidence from action-outcome predictions guides recurrent hypothesis updates without generating textual memory. A context-conditioned readout exposes hypotheses separately to the policy through a fixed-token belief prefix in the default configuration. The belief modules and policy are jointly trained using action imitation and auxiliary state, outcome, and observation-discrimination objectives. Across ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, LAMB matches or outperforms PABU, improving ALFWorld SR@30 and ScienceWorld success by 6.0 and 22.0 percentage points, respectively, and Crafter achievement progress by 26.37 points. On ALFWorld, it also reduces the redundant-action rate by 17.70 percentage points. These results support latent multi-hypothesis beliefs as compact memory for effective long-horizon decision making

Abstract: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.
title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models

Abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. To address this, we present MedPAO-Assist, an edge-deployable agentic framework that generates structured radiology reports directly from radiologist dictation and voice commands, requiring only $\approx3.3$ GB peak RAM and achieving an average end-to-end latency of $\approx31$ seconds on a standard laptop CPU through an asynchronous, multi-threaded execution pipeline. We evaluate each pipeline stage individually -- concept extraction, ontology grounding, and concept categorization and report hardware profiling results demonstrating the system's feasibility for real-time, CPU-only clinical deployment.

Whether you are iterating on a quick bug fix or planning a complex migration, different tasks call for different models.

In keeping with Google Cloud's commitment to an open ecosystem and to give developers the right model for every job, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are now available in Google Antigravity for Google Cloud customers. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for complex work while Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement.

Once enabled by an administrator, developers can select Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 directly from the model picker. Administrators can also select Google’s Gemini models, including Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon. The models apply across Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI and our recently released Antigravity IDE extensions for VS Code, JetBrains IntelliJ, and Visual Studio. This lets you choose the right model for the job, under a unified enterprise billing and security boundary.

In this post, we’ll share two engineering patterns for building in Antigravity using these models. To view the entire list of models supported in Antigravity across subscriptions, see our documentation here.

Multi-model engineering patterns in Antigravity

Having multiple model families available inside the same agent harness unlocks practical multi-model workflows that improve code quality while controlling latency and cost.

Pattern 1: Cross-model verification ("LLM-as-a-Judge") in loop and graph workflows

When building agentic loops or multi-step graph workflows, using the same model to both write code and review its own output can reinforce model-specific blind spots. Pairing two distinct model families, one as the implementer and another as the validator (judge), provides independent verification before moving to the next stage of a workflow.

In Antigravity, you can run this pattern either interactively or via automated subagents:

  1. Plan and implement with Model A: Start in planning mode using Claude Opus 5.5 or Gemini 4 Argon to design and implement a multi-file change.
  2. Validate with Model B: Before committing or advancing the loop, switch models, or invoke a one-shot /model check in the CLI, to have a different model family critique the implementation against your test suite and requirements.

Pattern 2: Pairing reasoning models with Flash subagents

Complex engineering tasks often combine a few high-reasoning decisions with dozens of high-volume, mechanical lookups (searching files, grepping logs, checking lint output, or classifying test failures). Running every lookup on a frontier model can increase both latency and spend.

Antigravity's Subagent customization system (.agents/agents/*.md) lets you assign specific model tiers (inherit, flash, or pro) to specialized subagents. When your primary session is running a more powerful model.

Subagents configured with model: inherit use your active session model for deep reasoning subtasks.

Subagents configured with model: flash offload high-speed search, classification, and triage work to Gemini Flash models.

For example, you can define a fast log-triage subagent in .agents/agents/test-triager.md:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '--- name: test-triager description: Runs unit tests, classifies failures, and returns a concise summary of failing assertions. model: flash tools: - read - edit --- Run the requested test targets, classify any failures by root cause (compilation error, assertion failure, or timeout), and return a structured summary to the parent agent.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f80f8acf610>)])]>

And a cross-model code reviewer subagent in .agents/agents/gemini-judge.md:

<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "--- name:cross-model-judge description: Independent LLM-as-a-judge verifier that audits diffs and edge cases using Gemini Pro. model: pro tools: - read --- Review the current workspace diff against the user's requirements. Check for regressions, missing edge-case tests, and security issues. Output a pass/fail verdict with specific line references."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f80f8ace290>)])]>

With this setup, you can delegate rapid test-and-classify loops to test-triager and trigger cross-model-judge to validate the final diff, combining the strengths of each model in a single workflow.

Getting started

Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 are available now for Google Cloud customers using Antigravity:

  1. Administrators (Gemini for business): Third-party partner models do not draw from the pooled Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus edition monthly token quota. Instead, usage is billed on a pay-as-you-go basis through your existing Google Cloud Billing account, so overages must be enabled. Visit “Gemini Enterprise” > “Settings” > “AI developer tools” in the Google Cloud Console to configure overage billing, spend limits and authorize partner models for your organization. See Configure AI developer tools settings for step-by-step instructions.
  2. Administrators (Gemini platform): You can also enable partner models if you are using Antigravity through the API in Gemini platform. Enable Claude models in Model Garden and complete the standard Anthropic terms.
  3. Developers: Update to the latest version of Antigravity 2.0, the Antigravity CLI, or the Antigravity IDE extensions, and open the model picker (or run /model) to select the right model for your task. To learn more about enterprise governance and multi-agent configuration, visit the Google Antigravity Enterprise documentation. You can switch the active model between turns in the same conversation thread while preserving workspace state, open artifacts, and terminal context.

Note: Lightweight first-party Gemini models continue to run in the background to handle high-frequency client-side coordination, such as context management and summaries. They consume first-party tokens and can incur charges.

  • Fixed /effort and /autocompact settings not applying when the model name differed from a modelOverrides value by letter case or a [1m] tag
  • Fixed new worktrees in a bare repository sometimes starting from local HEAD instead of the default branch, and unchanged subagent worktrees sometimes not being cleaned up

  • Fixed an MCP server passed by a cloud session or by the SDK's setMcpServers being replaced later in the session by a same-named server from your own settings

analysis.summary_cn: arXiv 提出 WaveCommitments，面向语音 Agent 生态中的资产交易市场：卖方出于隐私不能公开 embedding、频谱图或原始数据，买方又需先测试才能定价。该方案在可信执行环境（TEE）内用 Data Shapley 做保密估值，并结合多元多项式承诺实现选择性披露与防篡改溯源，证明交付资产与估值一致而隐藏其余内容。在 Whisper 等编码器、三个数据集上，基准速度最高提升 20 倍，证明体积最多缩小 39 倍。

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.26867v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern speech systems are evolving into ecosystems of autonomous speech agents that speak together, negotiate, and trade assets such as embeddings, spectrograms, or raw data. In such markets, sellers cannot reveal assets for evaluation due to privacy constraints, and buyers cannot price what they cannot test. Thus, we open-source WaveCommitments, an end-to-end design that pairs confidential asset valuation via Data Shapley inside a trusted execution environment with multivariate polynomial commitments. It enables selective openings and tamper-evident provenance to prove that a delivered asset matches the valuation while hiding everything else. Our extensive experiments across three known datasets and various tasks with state-of-the-art encoders, including Whisper, reveal that we speed up the best benchmarks by up to 20x while reducing their proof sizes by up to 39x. We also systematically study how a speaker's value shifts across tasks and encoders, revealing agent-level market prices.
title: WaveCommitments: Private and Verifiable Speech-Agent Marketplaces

raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.26952v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relational triple extraction identifies entity relations from raw sentences without depending on entity type information. The performance of traditional methods is seriously degenerated by ``unseen'' entities, because these methods can't build contextual dependencies relevant ``unseen'' entities. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a multi-granularity interaction network that leverages word-word, entity-relation, and head-tail interactions to capture deep semantic dependencies. By incorporating multiple iterations, the multi-granularity interaction network is effective to refine the representations corresponding to head and tail entities. It enhances the global semantic features associated with relational triples, aiding in the remediation of triples that may have been overlooked or omitted in earlier steps. Strong and consistent performance is achieved by our method on two rearranged datasets, with a significant improvement in identifying relational triples, including those involving ``unseen'' named entities. For example, our model improves F1-score by 3.1%/20.5% over previous approaches on the NYT-R/WebNLG-R datasets in the Unseen metric. Code: https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/Interaction-Network.
title: A Multi-granularity Interaction Network for Relational Triple Extraction

arXiv:2610.26899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.
title: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing

raw_summary:
My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.

  • Battle Drones
  • How I built this
  • v1: the initial prototype
  • v2: full sprites
  • v3: varied terrain
  • v4: the fun update
  • v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
  • v8: Archipelago
  • v10: Goliath, and agent battles
  • Agent battles
  • v11: Random Maps
  • v12: Multiplayer via sound
  • Some thoughts
  • Update: Online multiplayer support

Battle Drones

My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.

After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. (Update: also online multiplayer; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!)

Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser:

Features so far include:

  • 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here
  • Fog of war
  • Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles
  • Six maps, across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical
  • A random map generator
  • Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map
  • Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible
  • Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer
  • Crate drops with bonus resources
  • In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out
  • Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad)
  • AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other
  • The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base
  • Mutators that add extra rules or twists
  • A "Daily Op" challenge
  • Ranks and achievements (Medals)
  • Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other
  • A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong

How I built this

Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project.

Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts.

v1: the initial prototype

I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July:

We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources

Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions

Here's a shared transcript. I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites.

You can try v1 here - it looked like this:

It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against.

This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play.

Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later!

v2: full sprites

The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself.

Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder.

v3: varied terrain

It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it:

Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain.

This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this:

This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly.

v4: the fun update

So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play.

I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone:

This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.

This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as:

A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once.

This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular.

You can try v4 here - it looks like this:

I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights:

Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play.

  • Openers: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts.
  • Call-down powers: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike.
  • Objectives and salvage: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap.
  • Feel: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer.
  • Command: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement.
  • New modes: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign.
  • Progression: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op.

Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.

Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features.

v5: Battle Drones goes 3D

After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious:

Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes

That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version:

The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code.

v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft.

v8: Archipelago

I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases.

I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them.

It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map.

This resulted in my longest prompt yet:

Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles.

To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor.

Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board.

The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places

I want to encourage a battle over uplinks.

The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square

First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications

You get to design a new biome for this

The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this:

v10: Goliath, and agent battles

I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000.

Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude:

Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet

Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be.

Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops

Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it

[...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech

The end result is really cool.

Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map.

Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area.

Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map!

The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built.

There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths:

  • Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units.
  • Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one).

Agent battles

The other v10 feature is agent battles. In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game?

Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...]

Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin

Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles - here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna, and here's that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses.

The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here.

There are a few more replays like this linked in the README. I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future.

v11: Random Maps

This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target:

Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative.

Here's the transcript, and an image Claude generated to show me its work:

v12: Multiplayer via sound

I only just got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other!

This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept:

Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals

Build a version of that for battledrones

Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well!

Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game.

Some thoughts

I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results.

Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

This morning (via Hacker News) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop. I wouldn't personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this - it's still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project.

... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell).

I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!

A few other observations from this project:

  • Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out.
  • This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached.
  • Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts.
  • Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects.
  • For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay.
  • Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition.
  • I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked.
  • Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe, the Model browser, the Agent vs. Agent debug tool, and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven't even explored myself.
  • Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame).
  • Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt.
  • I'm still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from.

Update: Online multiplayer support

Earlier in this article I said:

Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

Then I tried playing the multiplayer version with Natalie... and the high pitched modem sounds gave her a nasty headache!

That's a pretty bad bug. I added a warning and was then inspired to build proper network multiplayer. I tried getting WebRTC to work but couldn't get a connection going between two of my own devices even on my own WiFi network, so I had Claude build a simple, stateless WebSockets relay server instead:

If I wanted to support multiplayer between two devices at a very low cost without storing any state on the server could I do that with a tiny asyncio web server running on the cheapest Fly instance?

Build the server and the fly.toml for deploying it, use Fly application name battledrones-relay - put that in a folder in the repo, include deploy instructions in the README in that folder

Here's the resulting server. Since this scales to zero and runs on a single Fly.io shared-cpu-1x instance it should cost me no more than $2.19/month - and that's if it stays hot and serving connections the whole time.

Battle Drones now supports online multiplayer. Click "Duel a friend online", then either share the resulting room URL via your messaging app of choice or have them snap a picture of the displayed QR Code.

I also added a feature where you can copy JSON of the match once it has ended and then feed that into the replay feature to rewatch your game.

I didn't expect to introduce online multiplayer this soon, but the headache bug felt like it warranted an urgent alternative.

raw_summary:
Earlier this month at Gemini at Work, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent for work. It answers your questions, handles your knowledge work, creates your images and media, and writes and runs code. You give it objectives, not instructions, and come back to finished work. It plans the work, uses skills and tools, connects to your systems, and has the security, administration, and governance your organization requires.

Every industry runs on knowledge a general model does not have. Government work runs on statute, regulation, and agency guidance, across siloed legacy systems, under strict requirements for data sovereignty, compliance, and confidentiality. Too often that leaves civil servants on data entry and manual document review instead of the services citizens depend on.

Today we're bringing the Gemini agent to public service with Gemini for government services in preview, part of our new suite of purpose-built industry solutions. It adds skills built around government work, connections to the systems agencies already run, and specialized partner agents, with governance running underneath it all.

Five components of Gemini for government services

Developed alongside agency leaders, Gemini for government services provides an integrated, fully governed environment configured for rapid deployment across federal, state, and local agencies with five core components:

  1. Skills for government work: Skills are reusable instructions and context, written by domain experts, that teach Gemini to run a specific task. Each one applies the statute, regulation, and agency guidance that govern that task, so an agency's standard operating procedures carry into the work Gemini supports.
  2. Connectors to agency systems: Secure connectors link Gemini to the case management, ERP, HR, and collaboration systems agencies already run, along with authoritative federal data sources. Gemini queries each system in place, so no data is migrated, and access follows the identity and permission controls the agency already has.
  3. Partner agents: Skills and connectors come together in agents, including pre-built agents from public sector software providers that agencies can deploy right away. They handle tasks like FOIA discovery and batch redaction under the same central governance, with a person approving each consequential step.
  4. A governed control plane: Security and compliance teams get one place to set and enforce policy across every agent, including VPC Service Controls, CMEK, and Assured Workloads. Outputs are grounded in source documents, with citations, so reviewers can check where each answer came from.
  5. An open partner ecosystem: Every agency works under a different statute and runs a different mix of systems. System integrators and public sector ISVs help agencies customize Gemini, connect it to what they already have, and scale it without lock-in.

Skills for government workflows

Gemini for government services helps automate and accelerate complex government operations, including:

  • Policy and regulatory research: Ask an operational or eligibility question and get an answer drawn from the CFR, the Federal Register, state administrative codes, and internal manuals, with page and paragraph citations. Where federal and state rules both apply, Gemini shows which one governs to empower agency decision makers.
  • FOIA record discovery: Gemini searches SharePoint, Drive, and email archives for records responsive to a FOIA or state Sunshine Law request. It organizes them into a review set for the records officer and agency counsel, shortening discovery that often takes weeks.
  • Redaction for public release: Gemini finds sensitive constituent data across a batch of documents, groups the findings so reviewers can clear them in passes, and proposes redactions labeled by statutory exemption. After a reviewer confirms, it produces the exemption log and audit-ready copies.
  • Vendor bid evaluation: Gemini checks multi-volume bids against RFP requirements, FAR guidelines, minimum mandatory criteria, and evaluation rubrics, and returns scoring justifications with citations. Contracting officers get a documented basis for each award decision.
  • Grant and program expense audits: Gemini checks invoices, receipts, purchase orders, and ledger entries against 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance and the terms of the award. It flags unallowable costs, missing documentation, and funding discrepancies with line-item citations, so problems surface while there's still time to fix them.
  • Document validation at intake: Gemini classifies and validates pay stubs, W-2s, utility bills, and leases when they arrive, checks the numbers for consistency, and flags missing signatures. Defects are caught before the application enters the queue, not weeks into the case.
  • Plain-language notices: Gemini turns policy memos and agency guidance into public notices, aligned to the Plain Writing Act of 2010, USDA-FNS standards, and Title VI language access guidance.

Open ecosystem of connectors across the government technology stack

Gemini for government services connects directly to core agency systems via secure connectors. Access is bound by existing role-based access controls, record-level permissions, and the trusted data controls inherited from each system — and nothing is migrated to make the connection work.

Federal regulatory and public data:

  • Federal Register: Tracks legislative actions, regulations, and executive orders as they post, so state and local teams see federal changes as they land.
  • regulations.gov: Tracks federal rulemaking dockets, public comments, and statutory agency response deadlines, keeping policy analysts ahead of incoming mandates.
  • eCFR (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations): Grounds answers in the governing regulation, with citations down to the paragraph.

Agency systems of record:

  • Oracle E-Business Suite: Gives agents permission-bound access to procurement, payables, and ledger transactions for expense auditing and award reconciliation.
  • Oracle PeopleSoft: Connects HR and personnel records under existing role-based controls, so workforce questions are answered from the system of record.
  • Salesforce: Enables conversational experiences across the Missionforce portfolio, including benefits, licensing and permitting, and contact center management.
  • ServiceNow: Automates IT, CRM, security, employee experience, and workflow records, so agents can track incidents, requests, and approval chains inside existing routing rules.

Productivity and collaboration:

  • Google Workspace: Connects with Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets to analyze case communications and agency correspondence and surface internal files while enforcing agency access controls.
  • Microsoft 365 and SharePoint: Integrates with Word, Outlook, and SharePoint to triage inquiries and ground responses in mail and intranet repositories without breaking workflow context.

Third-party agents and implementation partners

Every agency operates differently. Through our open platform, agencies can deploy pre-built partner agents or work with system integrators to scale custom capabilities:

  • SZNS Solutions FOIA and public records discovery agent: Turns a plain-language request, a piece of correspondence, or a formal citizen inquiry into a scoped search across enterprise archives — bounded by custodian and date range, so a records officer narrows the set before any data moves. It exports responsive material into secure agency repositories and tracks delivery status, giving each request an auditable trail from intake to release.
  • SZNS Solutions document redaction agent: Works inside connected repositories — SharePoint and Drive among them — finding sensitive citizen data across a batch and grouping the findings so a reviewer clears them in passes rather than page by page. Each proposed redaction carries its statutory exemption, and once the reviewer confirms, the agent exports permanently redacted, audit-ready copies back to the system of record, with the processing never leaving the agency's cloud perimeter.
  • Systems integrators & tech partners: Strategic partnerships with Accenture Federal Services, Clutch, Dark Wolf, Daston, Deloitte, Egen, Game Plan Tech, Knexus, Onix, Resultant, SAIC, Slalom, and SZNS Solutions so agencies can customize, integrate, and scale these capabilities without vendor lock-in.

Developed alongside federal, state, and local government agencies

We are working closely with select federal and state agencies, including the State of Missouri and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to ensure these capabilities work in day-to-day agency operations.

"Our citizens expect the government to move at the speed of modern life, not the speed of paperwork. By automating routine work in our workflows, we're delivering faster, better services to Missourians." - Tim Marczewski, Director of AI and Innovation, State of Missouri Office of Administration.

Built on an enterprise-grade foundation

Gemini for government services runs on Google Cloud's secure foundation, and can be deployed using the Assured Workloads FedRAMP High Data Boundary, enforcing U.S. data residency and personnel controls. It works within the authorities, retention rules, and approval chains your agency already has.

Agency records, constituent data, institutional documents, custom agents, and model outputs stay private to your organization, and are never used to train or fine-tune Google's foundation models without your permission. Because we operate the full stack, from infrastructure and models through the application layer, we can tune performance and cost together — routing high-volume document parsing and routine records sweeps to fast, low-cost models and reserving high-reasoning models for complex policy analysis, so expanding what your teams can take on does not mean expanding spend at the same rate.

This is just the beginning

The launch of Gemini for government services represents another defining step in delivering on our promise to bring the best of Gemini to every professional, for every workflow, natively tailored to the way they work.

Gemini for government services is available in preview today, joining our purpose-built solutions for industries. We invite leaders at every level of government to explore how Gemini can transform their most critical workflows.
